title: Redwood demo (latency/cost + Dedicated capacity) - Northstar Payments platform team
summary: Northstar Payments platform team saw Redwood’s hosted API demo focused on production economics: token-level latency/cost breakdown, batching and caching toggles, and how Dedicated capacity avoids noisy-neighbor behavior. Customer pushed on quota predictability, burst handling, and what Redwood can commit to (p95 latency, throughput) for peak payment events. Redwood positioned Hosted vs Dedicated, explained isolation (dedicated GPU pools), autoscaling/burst options, and demoed observability views with synthetic traffic. Next steps: share sizing worksheet + draft Dedicated configuration, schedule a deeper technical session on quotas/limits and SLOs, and align on a short POC with success criteria.
topics: Current Northstar workload and peak traffic patterns
Latency vs cost levers (batching/caching) and token-level breakdown
Noisy neighbor concerns and Dedicated isolation
Quota predictability, rate limits, and burst strategy
Dedicated capacity sizing assumptions (concurrency, tokens/sec, context lengths)
Observability: per-route dashboards, errors, and traces (synthetic demo traffic)
Security/compliance quick check (audit logs, RBAC, retention) - light touch
questions: How do you set and enforce quotas per project/user, and can we pre-negotiate burst?
What does Dedicated actually reserve (GPUs, tokens/sec), and what happens during regional capacity events?
How do we avoid p95 spikes when other tenants are busy (noisy neighbor)?
Can you commit to predictable throughput at peak (Black Friday / payroll days)?
What’s the typical delta in unit cost when batching/caching is tuned for our context distribution?
next_steps: Redwood to send Dedicated sizing template + a proposed baseline configuration for Northstar (including burst policy assumptions).
Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive on quota/rate-limit model, SLOs, and failover options (Avery to coordinate with Markus + Northstar SREs).
Northstar to share anonymized workload ranges: avg + p95 prompt length, max context, target completion length, and peak QPS/concurrency windows.
Redwood to follow up with pricing guidance: Hosted usage-based vs Dedicated commit ranges and what is included in SLA tiering.
Discuss a 2-week POC plan with success criteria (latency p95 target, max error rate, unit cost ceiling).
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-11-12
Start time: 2:00 PM ET
Duration: 47 min
Title: Redwood demo (latency/cost + Dedicated capacity) - Northstar Payments platform team
Attendees:
- Avery Johnson (Redwood, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Sales Engineering)
- Jenna Liu (Northstar Payments, Platform Eng Manager)
- Miguel Santos (Northstar Payments, SRE)
- Priya Raman (Northstar Payments, Staff SWE)
- Tom Becker (Northstar Payments, Finance/Procurement)
- Sarah Kim (Northstar Payments, Security Eng)

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making the time. I know we’ve got 45, 50 minutes. Goal today is to show you Redwood’s inference platform, but like, specifically through the lens you asked for: latency, cost predictability, and the Dedicated capacity story.

[00:13] Avery Johnson: Markus is gonna drive most of the clicks. I’ll do some framing and then we’ll leave time for Q&A. Sound good?

[00:19] Jenna Liu: Yep.

[00:20] Miguel Santos: Works.

[00:21] Priya Raman: Yeah.

[00:23] Markus Klein: Great. I’m gonna share my screen.

[00:27] (screen share starts)

[00:29] Avery Johnson: Quick context check before we dive in. Jenna, last time you mentioned you’re evaluating a few options—some managed endpoints, some self-hosting. What’s the main driver? Is it p95 latency or more cost or…?

[00:41] Jenna Liu: It’s both, but honestly predictability. We can eat a higher average if the spikes are controlled. We’ve had issues with multi-tenant stuff where p95 just goes sideways when everybody else is busy.

[00:53] Miguel Santos: Yeah, noisy neighbor. And quota behavior. Like we’ll get a 429 and it’s unclear if it’s our limit or the provider’s capacity.

[01:02] Avery Johnson: Got it. Noisy neighbor and “what does a 429 mean” are very common. That’s actually why we’ll spend extra time on Dedicated and on the quota/rate limit controls.

[01:12] Markus Klein: Okay, you should see the Redwood Console. This is our demo tenant, synthetic usage—so nothing customer-ish. I’m on the “Routes” view. We have a route pinned to a model version for stability.

[01:25] Priya Raman: You said pinned—like you can pin model versions, not just “latest”?

[01:29] Markus Klein: Exactly. You can pin a specific version, and then do controlled rollouts. For today we’re pinned so the demo doesn’t change under us.

[01:38] Avery Johnson: And in Dedicated, it’s the same concept—your route config and policies are consistent. The key change is capacity isolation.

[01:46] Markus Klein: I’ll start with a quick API call. This is chat completions with streaming. You’ll see tokens coming back.

[01:56] Markus Klein: (typing) I’m hitting our hosted endpoint first. Here’s the request payload—stream true, and we’ll request a structured output. Not perfect transcription here but you can see the schema.

[02:10] Markus Klein: (runs request)

[02:12] (streaming output begins)

[02:13] Markus Klein: So this is streaming chunk-by-chunk. Now, the part you care about is what the platform tells you about cost and latency. I’m switching over to the “Request details” panel.

[02:25] Miguel Santos: Are you showing token breakdown per request or aggregated?

[02:29] Markus Klein: Both. Per request you can see prompt tokens, completion tokens, time to first token, total latency, and then the effective cost. Then there’s an aggregate dashboard by route.

[02:40] Avery Johnson: The core idea is we give you levers—batching, caching—and we show the impact in the same UI. Otherwise you’re guessing.

[02:48] Markus Klein: Right. Here, time to first token is 280-ish ms for this request, total 1.7 seconds. Prompt tokens 420, completion 180.

[02:59] Priya Raman: What model is that?

[03:01] Markus Klein: In this demo it’s one of our curated open models in the catalog—think a “general chat” family. The exact name isn’t important. In your environment you’d pick the one that hits quality targets.

[03:12] Jenna Liu: Sorry to interrupt—do you do OpenAI compatibility or is it your own SDK?

[03:17] Markus Klein: Both. There’s an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and also native SDKs. For platform teams, a lot of folks start with compatibility and then move to native for specific controls.

[03:28] Avery Johnson: Okay, let’s pivot to what you asked for: production economics.

[03:33] Markus Klein: Yeah. I’m on “Optimize” settings for this route. Two toggles: continuous batching and prefix caching. These are simplified in demo, but in real configs you can tune thresholds.

[03:45] Miguel Santos: Continuous batching meaning you batch multiple user requests onto a single GPU pass?

[03:49] Markus Klein: Exactly. It improves throughput and reduces per-token cost, with some tradeoff in tail latency depending on workload.

[03:57] Markus Klein: I’m going to run the same prompt set with batching off, then on, and you’ll see the delta in the dashboard.

[04:05] Priya Raman: Is this synthetic traffic generator you mentioned earlier?

[04:08] Markus Klein: Yep. For the demo we have a job that sends a known distribution—short prompts, medium prompts, some long contexts. That keeps charts populated.

[04:17] Markus Klein: (clicks) First run: batching OFF, caching OFF.

[04:22] (pause)

[04:24] Markus Klein: Switching to the “Cost & Latency” dashboard. You’ll see two minutes windows, p50/p95, and cost per 1K tokens effective.

[04:35] Tom Becker: When you say cost per 1K tokens, is that like list pricing, or actual?

[04:40] Avery Johnson: Good question. In the console, this is based on your contracted rates and the measured tokens. In demo, it’s using placeholder rates, but conceptually it maps to actual billable usage.

[04:52] Tom Becker: Okay.

[04:53] Markus Klein: Here’s the baseline. Now I turn batching ON.

[04:58] Markus Klein: (clicks)

[05:00] Markus Klein: Kicking the same workload.

[05:05] Miguel Santos: But doesn’t batching add queueing? That’s where p95 gets hurt.

[05:10] Markus Klein: It can, yes. The point is you decide. For latency-sensitive traffic you can keep it off, or have separate routes: one “low-latency” route, one “cheap throughput” route.

[05:22] Avery Johnson: A lot of customers run two classes: interactive and background. Same model, different route policy.

[05:30] Markus Klein: Okay charts updated. See p50 latency basically flat, p95 slightly higher, but cost per token drops. Again, these numbers are demo-ish, but directionally correct.

[05:44] Priya Raman: Do you show it per customer or per API key? We need internal chargeback.

[05:48] Markus Klein: You can segment by project, key, route, and tag. For enterprise we support usage export too.

[05:56] Miguel Santos: Can you export to Datadog? We’re heavy on that.

[05:59] Markus Klein: Yeah, we have tracing hooks and metrics export. For the demo environment we keep it inside the console, but in real you can pipe it out.

[06:10] Jenna Liu: Okay, but the big thing is still: hosted multi-tenant. How do I know I don’t get p95 spikes because someone else is doing a giant batch job.

[06:19] Avery Johnson: Yep. That’s the Dedicated conversation.

[06:22] Markus Klein: I’ll explain it and then show the controls. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools—isolated capacity. Your traffic isn’t sharing GPU time with other tenants.

[06:33] Miguel Santos: Like literally dedicated A100s or whatever? Or “dedicated quota” on shared?

[06:37] Markus Klein: Dedicated GPU pool. The underlying hardware can vary, but it’s not a shared multi-tenant runtime. It’s reserved capacity with an SLO.

[06:47] Avery Johnson: And you get predictable throughput. Also, quotas become your choice. Like you can define project-level limits and bursts, rather than hitting a provider’s global cap.

[06:59] Priya Raman: What about if the region is out of capacity? Like all the GPUs are taken.

[07:04] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, we reserve. So the “out of capacity” scenario is much less likely unless you exceed what you reserved. For bursting, there are options: pre-negotiated burst into a secondary pool, or fallback to compatible model/region.

[07:18] Jenna Liu: Fallback to another region could be an issue for us.

[07:21] Avery Johnson: Understood. In payments, sometimes you need data locality. But there’s also intra-region failover, and model-variant fallback without moving regions.

[07:32] Miguel Santos: Okay but then quotas. We had an incident with another provider: we were under our purchased limit but got rate limited because their internal capacity was tight. How do you avoid that?

[07:44] Markus Klein: In Dedicated, the limit is your reserved pool. So if we agree you have X tokens/sec and Y concurrency, that’s yours. If you exceed, you’d see a clear signal: you’re above your plan, not “mystery 429.”

[07:59] Avery Johnson: And if you want burst, we can define that as part of the contract: “up to 2x for 15 minutes” type of thing. Not promising here live, but that’s the pattern.

[08:10] Tom Becker: I’m gonna jump in—when you say contract, are we talking an annual commit for Dedicated?

[08:16] Avery Johnson: Typically monthly or annual commits, yeah. There’s a few structures. Hosted stays usage-based. Dedicated is reserved capacity pricing.

[08:26] Tom Becker: Okay.

[08:27] Markus Klein: Let me show Dedicated-like controls in the console. In demo we don’t actually spin real dedicated GPUs for every click, but the config mirrors what you’d have.

[08:38] Markus Klein: Here’s “Capacity policy” for the route: target concurrency, max queue, request timeout behavior, and an optional fallback policy.

[08:48] Sarah Kim: Can you audit who changes these settings?

[08:51] Markus Klein: Yes—audit logs track config changes, key creation, role changes.

[08:57] Avery Johnson: For today we won’t go deep on security docs unless you want, but yes: audit logs + RBAC.

[09:05] Sarah Kim: Okay. Just wanted to make sure.

[09:07] Markus Klein: Now, noisy neighbor specifically—here’s a “hosted vs dedicated” comparison panel. In hosted, we enforce fairness across tenants. In dedicated, fairness is inside your org, not across orgs.

[09:21] Miguel Santos: That’s good. But like, what’s the SLO you can offer? We’d need p95 under, say, 900ms for certain prompts.

[09:30] Avery Johnson: We can talk SLOs, but it depends on model, context length, region. What we do in a POC is measure your distribution and then propose an SLO + sizing.

[09:42] Markus Klein: Yeah, we don’t want to hand-wave. If your prompts are 4k context and long completions, the numbers are different.

[09:50] Priya Raman: Our typical is 600 to 1,200 tokens prompt, completion 200-ish. But we have spikes.

[09:57] Miguel Santos: And some batch jobs that do longer—like 8k.

[10:02] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. In a sizing exercise we’d separate interactive from batch. That’s usually the key.

[10:10] Avery Johnson: Also, you mentioned “peak payment events.” Is that like end of month? Or Black Friday? What’s the pattern.

[10:18] Jenna Liu: End of month and like payroll Fridays. Also certain partner events. It’s not totally predictable.

[10:26] Avery Johnson: So you need burst tolerance.

[10:28] Jenna Liu: Exactly.

[10:29] Markus Klein: One approach: reserve for baseline and define burst to a secondary pool. Another: keep hosted for non-critical workloads and dedicated for critical. Depends on your risk appetite.

[10:43] Miguel Santos: If hosted is still multi-tenant, we’d only use it for non-prod.

[10:46] Markus Klein: That’s common.

[10:48] Avery Johnson: Let’s do a quick “what happens when capacity is constrained” demo. Markus, can you trigger the fallback?

[10:54] Markus Klein: Yep. In the demo we simulate a constrained primary by setting max concurrency to 1 and then sending a burst.

[11:03] Markus Klein: (clicking) Setting route concurrency low.

[11:07] Markus Klein: Running 20 parallel requests.

[11:10] (background noise)

[11:12] Markus Klein: You’ll see some requests succeed on primary, others follow policy. Here the policy is “fallback to compatible variant in same family.”

[11:22] Priya Raman: Does that change output quality?

[11:24] Markus Klein: It can. That’s why you control which fallbacks are allowed. In payments you might prefer “fail fast” over quality shift.

[11:34] Jenna Liu: We probably need deterministic behavior.

[11:36] Markus Klein: Totally. For some routes you’d disable fallback and rely on reserved capacity sizing.

[11:44] Miguel Santos: So then how do you do error messaging? Like is it 429? 503?

[11:49] Markus Klein: You can configure. Typically “capacity exceeded” yields 429 with a specific error code, and you can include retry-after. But we can align with what your client expects.

[12:02] Avery Johnson: The key is: it’s not a mystery 429. It’s “you exceeded your configured limit.”

[12:08] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[12:10] Markus Klein: Here’s the request log. You can see “routed_to=primary” vs “routed_to=fallback.” And time to first token for each.

[12:20] Priya Raman: That routing label is helpful.

[12:22] Markus Klein: And on the aggregated dashboard, you can segment on routed_to.

[12:28] Tom Becker: Can you explain Dedicated in terms of cost? Like if we reserve, are we paying for idle.

[12:35] Avery Johnson: Yes, it’s like reserved capacity: you pay for the pool. The trade is predictability. We can do smaller pools and autoscale within a ceiling, but it’s not purely pay-per-token.

[12:50] Tom Becker: Okay, and do you offer like a hybrid where there’s a base and then per-token overage.

[12:55] Avery Johnson: There are structures like that. Usually it’s base commit + burst usage, depending.

[13:02] Jenna Liu: I want to make sure we’re not buying something where we still get throttled at peak.

[13:07] Avery Johnson: Understood. The contract is designed to make that explicit: if you reserve X, you should get X.

[13:15] Miguel Santos: But you said hardware can vary. If you move us from one GPU type to another, we lose predictability.

[13:22] Markus Klein: Good catch. We typically keep a pool consistent. If there’s a change, it’s planned and communicated. Also you measure in tokens/sec and latency, not GPU brand.

[13:34] Miguel Santos: Sure but the kernels behave differently.

[13:36] Markus Klein: They do. Our runtime selects kernels based on hardware. For Dedicated, we pin the underlying profile in the environment. It’s not “surprise” changes.

[13:48] Avery Johnson: In the POC we’ll also document the “known-good” configuration. That becomes the baseline for production.

[13:56] Priya Raman: What about context caching, like KV cache. Is that shared between requests? Any risk?

[14:03] Markus Klein: Great question. Prefix caching can reuse compute for identical prefixes, but it’s within your tenant boundary. Dedicated makes that cleaner because it’s your pool. In hosted, it’s still tenant-isolated.

[14:17] Sarah Kim: Tenant-isolated meaning no cross-customer data mixing.

[14:20] Markus Klein: Correct. No cross-customer cache reuse. It’s logically separated.

[14:25] Avery Johnson: I know security can go deep, but for today we’re focusing on performance and predictability.

[14:31] Jenna Liu: Can you show the “quota predictability” settings? Like per project.

[14:36] Markus Klein: Yup. Here’s “Rate limits.” You can set per API key, per project, per route. This is in tokens/minute, requests/minute, and concurrent streams. Also separate limits for streaming.

[14:50] Miguel Santos: That’s nice. Our provider today just has requests/minute and it doesn’t map to tokens.

[14:55] Markus Klein: Yeah, tokens is more realistic.

[14:58] Priya Raman: If we have multiple internal teams, can we allocate budgets.

[15:02] Markus Klein: You can set quotas and also alerts when someone burns budget.

[15:07] Avery Johnson: And because we’re trying to make demos realistic—this console view is what your platform team would use for internal governance.

[15:16] Miguel Santos: Okay but one thing: when we exceed, do we get immediate hard fail? Or can it queue.

[15:21] Markus Klein: Configurable. For interactive, you usually hard fail quickly with retry-after. For batch, you may queue. You can also set max queue time.

[15:33] Jenna Liu: I’d want a hard ceiling for prod so one bad deploy doesn’t eat everything.

[15:37] Markus Klein: That’s exactly the use case.

[15:40] Avery Johnson: Markus, can you show the “token-level breakdown” view you mentioned?

[15:44] Markus Klein: Yeah. Clicking into one request. Here’s a chart: time to first token, decode time, and also server-side queue time.

[15:54] Miguel Santos: Queue time is key. That’s what we need to monitor.

[15:58] Markus Klein: Yep, and if batching is on, you’ll see queue time go up a bit.

[16:05] Priya Raman: Is there a way to correlate with our request id.

[16:08] Markus Klein: We pass through your request id header and show it in logs. There’s also trace IDs.

[16:15] Avery Johnson: Let’s pause—any other big objections you want to make sure we address today?

[16:20] Jenna Liu: Dedicated capacity is interesting. But we need confidence on two things: (1) you can meet peak, and (2) the spend isn’t crazy.

[16:30] Tom Becker: Yeah, cost predictability for finance.

[16:33] Miguel Santos: And for SRE: clear signals. No mystery 429s. And if you do throttle, we want to know why.

[16:42] Avery Johnson: Perfect. So next step is usually: you share your workload ranges, we run a sizing pass, and we propose a Dedicated pool that hits your p95 and throughput targets. Then we do a short POC.

[16:56] Priya Raman: How short is short.

[16:58] Avery Johnson: Two weeks is common for performance validation if security isn’t blocking. Sometimes it’s longer if you need SSO and all that.

[17:06] Sarah Kim: For POC we might not need full SSO, but we’ll need at least RBAC and audit logs.

[17:11] Avery Johnson: That’s doable.

[17:13] Markus Klein: Also, we can do a dedicated test environment isolated from other customers for the POC. That addresses noisy neighbor during evaluation too.

[17:22] Miguel Santos: Okay. One more thing: we’re comparing to Bedrock and also maybe Together. Bedrock gives us some comfort because it’s AWS, but their quotas are… weird.

[17:33] Avery Johnson: Yep. We hear that. Bedrock’s quotas can be region-by-region and model-by-model, and it’s not always aligned to your real workload. Our stance is: quotas should map to tokens and the capacity you’ve reserved.

[17:47] Jenna Liu: And OpenAI? We use them for some stuff now.

[17:50] Avery Johnson: OpenAI is great for speed of integration, but for strict latency and predictability at scale, many teams end up wanting more control: dedicated capacity, per-route policies, detailed breakdowns.

[18:02] Markus Klein: If it helps, we can run the same prompt set across providers. But we try to keep it apples-to-apples.

[18:10] Priya Raman: We already have an eval harness. Could we plug in.

[18:13] Markus Klein: Yes. We support prompt sets and regression checks. In our console there’s an evals feature, but you can also use your harness.

[18:22] Miguel Santos: If you do a fallback to a different model variant, do you record that in the logs for later debugging.

[18:28] Markus Klein: Yes, you saw “routed_to” plus the model id/version used.

[18:34] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[18:36] Avery Johnson: I’m watching time. Markus, maybe do a quick wrap with the “Dedicated capacity sizing knobs.”

[18:42] Markus Klein: Sure. These are the three inputs we need: (1) prompt length distribution, (2) completion length distribution, (3) concurrency/QPS over time. Then we propose pool size. For Dedicated you can choose region, and optionally have a warm standby.

[18:58] Jenna Liu: Warm standby in same region.

[19:00] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[19:02] Tom Becker: Is warm standby extra cost.

[19:04] Avery Johnson: Typically yes, because it’s reserved. Sometimes it’s smaller capacity.

[19:10] Priya Raman: Do you support private VPC deployment. Not necessarily now, but long term.

[19:15] Avery Johnson: Yes, we have private deployments (VPC/on-prem) as an option. Dedicated is often the first step, and Private is for more regulated requirements.

[19:26] Sarah Kim: We’re not there yet, but good to know.

[19:29] Miguel Santos: When you say dedicated pool, does it include the control plane and the UI? Or is that still shared.

[19:35] Markus Klein: The control plane is multi-tenant but logically isolated. The data plane GPUs are dedicated. For Private, control plane can be private as well.

[19:46] Miguel Santos: Okay. As long as data plane is isolated, that’s what I care about.

[19:52] Avery Johnson: We can send an architecture one-pager after.

[19:55] Jenna Liu: Please.

[19:57] Avery Johnson: Alright, I think we’ve covered the main points. Let’s do a quick round: any final questions.

[20:03] Priya Raman: Just one—streaming reliability. We saw disconnects with another provider in EU. Do you have issues.

[20:09] Markus Klein: Generally stable. If there are region-specific issues, we’ll be transparent. In Dedicated, you can also keep it to one region and tune timeouts.

[20:20] Miguel Santos: Can we get SLAs in writing for Dedicated.

[20:23] Avery Johnson: Yes. Once we scope, we’ll share the SLA options.

[20:28] Tom Becker: And pricing ranges.

[20:30] Avery Johnson: Yep. I’ll send a follow-up with a rough range once we have your workload numbers. I don’t want to guess wildly.

[20:38] Jenna Liu: Okay, next step is we send you distributions.

[20:41] Avery Johnson: Exactly. I’ll email a template: prompt tokens p50/p95/max, completion p50/p95/max, peak concurrency window, and required p95 latency target. Then we’ll schedule a technical deep dive—maybe next week.

[20:55] Miguel Santos: Works.

[20:56] Priya Raman: Sounds good.

[20:58] Sarah Kim: And send the security/audit log doc.

[21:01] Avery Johnson: Will do.

[21:03] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[21:05] (call continues with scheduling chatter, partial transcription)

[21:06] Avery Johnson: Jenna, what does Tuesday look like—

[21:08] Jenna Liu: Tuesday morning is blocked, maybe Wednesday.

[21:11] Avery Johnson: Okay I’ll send two options.

[21:13] (end of captured transcript)

Note: Fireflies transcript ended early due to recording stop; remainder was scheduling logistics.
